title: Data Collection & Labeling
html:
A model can only be as good as its data. The training set must represent the population the model will serve, and the labels must be consistent enough to learn from.

Where data comes from

SourceStrengthsWatch out for
Product logs & databasesReal, plentiful, matches productionLogging bugs, missing fields, only sees what the current system shows users
Public datasetsFast to start, benchmarksDifferent population; license terms
APIs & web scrapingBroad coverageTerms of service, copyright, personal data, rate limits
Sensors / IoTHigh volume, time-stampedDrift, calibration errors, gaps
Human annotationLabels exactly what you needCost, inconsistency, annotator bias
Synthetic dataRare cases, privacyMay not reflect real-world messiness

Representativeness and sampling bias

  • Selection bias — the sample isn't random: a loan model trained only on approved applicants never sees how rejected ones would have repaid.
  • Survivorship bias — only the survivors are recorded (products still on sale, companies still trading).
  • Coverage gaps — a speech model trained on one accent, a vision model trained on daytime photos.
  • Time mismatch — data from last year when behaviour has since changed.
Key point

Ask: would the rows I train on look like the rows the model will score next month? If not, fix the collection before tuning any model.

Labeling

1
Write guidelines
Exact definitions and edge cases (“is a sarcastic review negative?”) with examples.
2
Pilot and measure agreement
Several annotators label the same items; compute inter-annotator agreement.
3
Label at scale with checks
Gold questions with known answers, multiple labels per item, majority vote or a label model.
4
Audit
Review disagreements and model–label conflicts; they often reveal unclear guidelines.

Raw percent agreement is inflated by chance. Cohen's kappa corrects for the agreement two annotators would reach by guessing with their own label frequencies:

κ = (pₒ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ) pₒ = observed agreement, pₑ = agreement expected by chance

Rough reading (Landis & Koch): < 0.4 poor to fair, 0.4–0.6 moderate, 0.6–0.8 substantial, > 0.8 near-perfect. Use Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha for more than two annotators.

Getting labels cheaply

Active learning

Train on a few labels, then ask humans to label the examples the model is least sure about — they carry the most information per label.

Weak supervision

Write several noisy labeling functions (keywords, regexes, heuristics, existing models); a label model estimates each function's accuracy and combines their votes into probabilistic labels (the Snorkel approach).

Semi-supervised

Use many unlabelled rows alongside a few labelled ones, e.g. self-training on confident predictions.

Transfer learning

Start from a model pre-trained on related data so far fewer labels are needed (see Deep Learning).

Watch out

Keep the raw data, the labeling guidelines and each dataset version together (DVC, lakeFS, or dated snapshots). A model whose training data can't be reproduced can't be debugged or audited.

How do you handle noisy labels?

Measure them first (agreement on a double-labelled sample). Then clarify guidelines, use several annotators with majority vote, review items where the model confidently disagrees with the label, and prefer models/losses that are robust to some noise. A clean, trustworthy test set matters most — you can't measure progress against wrong answers.

What is active learning?

An iterative loop: train on the current labels, score the unlabelled pool, send the most informative examples (usually the most uncertain) to annotators, add them and retrain. It reaches a target accuracy with fewer labels than random sampling.
